prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map supports a coarse room layout: walls, doorway edges, ceiling, and nearby foreground surfaces are bright, while the open room and people farther ahead are darker; across frames 1–3, most people and furniture appear roughly 2–5 m from the wearer, with walls and ceiling boundaries generally closer than the far room. In frame 4, a person or foreground body occupies much of the central view at approximately arm’s length to 1.5 m, occluding the room behind, while frame 5 points downward toward furniture and people about 1–3 m away. It makes the approach toward the close foreground figure and the change from forward-facing to downward-looking view clearer than RGB alone, and distinguishes near structural surfaces from deeper openings. Absolute metre estimates are unreliable because the monocular map has broad halos, weak object boundaries, and likely assigns some bright walls, ceiling regions, and silhouettes inconsistent depths.
descriptions.segmentation: The masks isolate people and chairs: frame 1 has no confident instance, frame 2 shows one person ahead-left and a chair farther right, frame 3 shows several partly overlapping people across the centre plus a chair to their right, frame 4 shows one large person directly ahead, and frame 5 shows a chair left-of-centre with people near the centre-right and extreme right edge. Mask size and overlap indicate that the frame-4 person is closest, roughly 0.5–1.5 m away, while most frame-2/3 people and chairs are roughly 2–5 m away; in frame 3, two central people are close to one another and partially occlude each other. The map makes the number, lateral ordering, partial truncation, and foreground occlusions easier to see than RGB, especially where lighting and motion blur obscure boundaries. It does not reliably show facing direction or gaze, misses much of the furniture and some visible people, merges or fragments overlapping silhouettes, and the frame-5 instances are partly out of view.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects a body skeleton only in frame 2 and another in frame 5, placing the first person ahead near the centre-right at roughly 2–4 m and the later person on the right side at roughly 1–3 m as the camera turns and tilts downward. In frame 2 the detected torso is approximately upright, with limbs extending below and to either side; in frame 5 the skeleton is strongly tilted in the image, with one long limb extending up-right, but the camera rotation makes world-relative above/below and standing orientation uncertain. It clarifies joint arrangement, limb reach, and body orientation where RGB silhouettes are dark or blurred, and suggests that neither detected person’s limbs extend into the wearer’s immediate arm’s-reach zone. The map is highly incomplete: it omits most visible people, shows no reliable hand skeletons, cannot establish gaze or whether faces point toward the wearer, and may misplace joints because of occlusion, cropping, blur, and the rotated final view.
